item.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=mechanical+constraint+enforcement+and+state+integrity+in+persistent+LLM+agent+memory+architectures&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6137731\", \"title\": [\"Architectures for Persistent Reasoning with Explicit World-State Representations in LLM-Based Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p><p>Building on a previously proposed five-layer cognitive architecture (EGI) for multi-agent <strong>LLM-based</strong> systems (Wang, 2026), this paper examines the role of explicit semantic world-state representations in enabling persistent and interpretable reasoning. Large language models (LLMs) have become foundational components of modern AI systems, enabling a wide range of practical applications across enterprises and analytical domains. In particular, LLM-based systems are widely used to support document-centric workflows such as information retrieval, question answering, summarization, and contextual explanation, which form critical inputs to analytical and decision-oriented tasks. As AI systems are increasingly applied to complex domains—including risk analysis, policy evaluation, and strategic decision support—additional cognitive requirements emerge beyond information access alone.</p>\\n<p>Many real-world applications require sustained reasoning across multiple analytical steps, integration of heterogeneous signals, and consistency of interpretation over time. While existing LLM-based pipelines effectively ground responses in external knowledge, they typically lack explicit mechanisms for maintaining and coordinating internal state across reasoning processes. As a result, analytical coherence often depends on ad hoc prompt design or external orchestration logic.</p>\\n<p>This paper introduces an architectural approach that extends LLM-based systems with explicit shared cognitive state. The proposed design treats internal semantic state as a first-class system component that can be updated, shared, and reasoned over by different modules or agents. By separating knowledge access from cognitive state management, the architecture enables more stable, coherent, and interpretable reasoning in analytical settings. The paper describes …
